name: Creatine for sleep deprivation
lead: Creatine is an organic compound that helps regenerate ATP in muscle and brain tissue and is widely sold as a dietary supplement.[1] Some people in fitness and looksmaxxing circles claim it can offset the cognitive effects of lost sleep.

Small experimental studies have examined this. A 2007 study tested creatine supplementation alongside sleep deprivation and exercise on cognition, mood and hormones,[2] and a 2026 study reported that a single dose reduced sleep-deprivation-related deterioration in cognitive performance.[3] Reviews of creatine and cognition more broadly report mixed results and an EFSA opinion that a cause-and-effect link cannot be established.[1] None of this concerns facial appearance.

paras: About 95 percent of the body's creatine is held in skeletal muscle, and the body also makes it from glycine and arginine.[1] Chevreul isolated it from muscle in 1832, and it gained public attention as a performance supplement after the 1992 Barcelona Olympics.[1]

Wikipedia summarizes the evidence as hard to interpret, with benefit possibly greatest in people under stress such as sleep deprivation.[1] A 2018 systematic review found possible improvement in short-term memory and reasoning, a 2023 meta-analysis of eight trials found improved memory, and a 2024 systematic review found no significant effect in healthy unstressed people and mixed results under stress.[1]

Common reported effects are water-retention weight gain and stomach upset; a 2019 National Kidney Foundation review found no kidney damage in healthy people at standard doses.[1] Safety data are lacking for children and pregnancy.[1]

A 2007 study gave creatine or placebo to participants before a sleep-deprivation protocol with intermittent exercise and measured cognitive and psychomotor performance, mood, effort and salivary cortisol and melatonin.[2] A 2026 study from the same research line examined a lower single dose during sleep deprivation, building on a previous study that reported changes in brain metabolism and reduced cognitive deterioration.[3] Effects on how a person looks have not been studied.

card.summary: Creatine taken to blunt the cognitive hit of lost sleep: small studies exist, nothing on looks.
card.note: Evidence concerns cognition, not appearance; reviews are mixed.

quick.overview:
Creatine is a common muscle supplement. Some claim it helps the brain cope with sleep deprivation.

A few small experiments have tested this on cognitive tests; none tested appearance.
quick.mechanism: Creatine helps regenerate ATP in muscle and brain, and researchers have proposed it may support brain energy metabolism under stress.[1][3]
quick.risks: At standard doses reviews report mainly water-retention weight gain and stomach upset, with no kidney damage in healthy people; data are lacking for children and pregnancy.[1]
